title: Securing Your Social Media Accounts: Facebook, Instagram, X, and More
excerpt: Social media account takeovers are used to scam your friends, spread misinformation, and conduct fraud under your identity. Here's how to lock down every major platform.
content:
What Attackers Do With Your Social Media Accounts

Losing access to a social media account isn't just embarrassing — it's actively dangerous. Attackers who take over accounts typically:

  • Message your friends and followers pretending to be you, asking for money or gift cards ('I'm stuck abroad and need emergency help')
  • Post crypto investment scams that appear to come from you
  • Sell access to accounts with large followings on underground markets
  • Use the accounts to spread misinformation or malware
  • Extract personal information from your messages and use it for further attacks

The attack surface is significant: Facebook has had multiple major breaches, Instagram accounts are stolen daily via SIM swapping and phishing, and LinkedIn credentials are heavily targeted for corporate espionage. Each platform deserves proper security configuration.

Passwords: Unique on Every Platform

Use a different password for every social media account. If you use the same password across Instagram, Facebook, X, LinkedIn, and TikTok, a breach on any one of them gives attackers access to all of them. Use our password generator to create a 20+ character random password for each and store them in a password manager.

Never use passwords that include your name, your pet's name, your birthday, or any real word — these are the first things targeted in dictionary attacks.

Platform-Specific Security Settings

Facebook: Settings & Privacy → Settings → Security and Login. Turn on two-factor authentication (use an authenticator app, not SMS). Enable login alerts — you'll get a notification if someone logs into your account from a new device or location. Review the 'Where you're logged in' section and log out any sessions you don't recognize.

Instagram: Profile → Menu → Settings → Accounts Center → Password and Security. Enable two-factor authentication. Check 'Login activity' for unfamiliar sessions. Note: Instagram is one of the most phished platforms — never enter your credentials anywhere except the official app or instagram.com.

X (Twitter): Settings → Security and account access → Security. Enable two-factor authentication (currently requires a subscription for authenticator app use, otherwise SMS). Enable 'Password reset protect' — this requires your email or phone to be confirmed before initiating a reset.

LinkedIn: Settings & Privacy → Sign in & security → Two-step verification. Enable it with an authenticator app. LinkedIn credentials are particularly valuable for spear phishing attacks against companies, as attackers use verified job titles and company affiliations to craft convincing emails.

TikTok: Profile → Menu → Settings and Privacy → Security → 2-step verification. Enable it. Also check 'Manage devices' for any unrecognized sessions.

Don't Use 'Login with Facebook' or 'Login with Google' Recklessly

Social login buttons ('Continue with Google', 'Login with Facebook') create a chain: if your Google or Facebook account gets compromised, every account using that social login is also compromised. For high-value accounts (banking, crypto, work tools), always create a dedicated account with a unique email and password instead.

If you've used social login widely and want to untangle it: Facebook → Settings → Apps and Websites shows every third-party app connected to your account. Review and remove any you don't actively use.

Recognizing Account Takeover Attempts

Watch for these warning signs that your account may be under attack or already compromised:

  • Password reset emails you didn't request — someone is trying to reset your password
  • Login notification from an unfamiliar device or location
  • Friends messaging you asking why you sent them a strange message
  • Posts appearing on your profile that you didn't make
  • Being logged out of your account unexpectedly

If you suspect your account has been taken over: use the platform's account recovery process immediately, change your password from a clean device, and check whether your recovery email or phone number has been changed.

Privacy Settings That Reduce Your Attack Surface

Reducing what attackers can learn about you limits how effectively they can social engineer you or guess your security answers:

  • Make your friends list private (on Facebook) — this limits information available for spear phishing
  • Remove your phone number from public profiles
  • Don't post details that answer common security questions: your mother's maiden name, your high school, your first car, your birthplace
  • Be cautious of those viral 'quiz' posts that ask for childhood details — they're often data harvesting

Recommended Tools

A password manager handles unique passwords across all your platforms without the mental overhead. NordPass is an excellent free option with a data breach scanner. 1Password's Watchtower feature flags any of your accounts that have appeared in known breaches.
